insights.explanation: The Rangpur piezometer taps the confined system at about 100-120 m depth, within Mansa's stacked sequence of Phreatic 0-70 m, Confined I 100-150 m, Confined II 185-210 m and Confined III 260-300 m, listed as suitable for drinking and irrigation.

insights.title: Mixed water-level signals around Mansa
insights.explanation: Seasonal May/October hydrographs from 2007-2017 exist for Rangpur, while other Mansa Confined Group-II stations diverged over 2008-2017 with one rising trend and one falling trend, indicating locally variable pressure behaviour.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of a district-wide pre-monsoon 2017 assessment of confined groundwater quality and decade-long seasonal level monitoring.

narrative.headline: Mid-range deep salinity at Rancharada amid sharp local contrasts and a falling level signal
narrative.summary: Rancharada's deep tube well recorded 740 mg/L dissolved solids in May 2017, in the lower-middle range for Kalol's confined aquifer. That relative freshness stands out against extreme nearby highs above 3,000 mg/L, but the same Group-II aquifer shows a 2008-2017 falling-level signal that tempers the picture.
narrative.why_it_matters: For siting or investment, Rancharada looks more usable than the highly saline pockets nearby, but the patchy salinity and falling deep-level signal mean quality and yield cannot be assumed across distance or time without site-specific testing and ongoing monitoring.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Rancharada as a lighter, moderate-salinity spot among darker high-TDS neighbours like Nasmed and Dingucha-I, while remembering its plotted point is approximate and its deep levels show a downward signal.

insights.title: Confined-aquifer salinity: 740 mg/L in May 2017
insights.explanation: The Rancharada tube well in Kalol taluka recorded 740 mg/L dissolved solids in the confined aquifer in May 2017. It comes from the systematic pre-monsoon 2017 survey of user-aquifer tube wells.

insights.title: Mid-range locally amid extreme salinity patchiness
insights.explanation: Nearby Kalol stations in the same May 2017 confined dataset range from 430 mg/L at Dingucha-II and 830 mg/L at Limbodara to 960 mg/L at Bhoyan Moti, 1,590 mg/L at Dingucha-I, and 3,210 mg/L at Nasmed. Rancharada sits in the lower-middle of that spread, showing how quickly deep quality changes over short distances.

insights.title: Deep Group-II levels flagged as falling, 2008-2017
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II at Rancharada, the 2008-2017 record reports a trend value of -1.60879 with a Fall direction. The record is flagged as needs review, so it is a cautionary signal rather than a final rate.

insights.title: Monitored tube well with approximate map position
insights.explanation: The quality value is mapped as part of the regional tube-well monitoring and TDS mapping effort. The longitude for Rancharada is truncated and flagged low-precision, so treat the map point as approximate within the village area.

narrative.secondary_context: Kalol taluka, Gandhinagar district; pre-monsoon May 2017 user-aquifer TDS survey; Confined Aquifer Group-II level trend 2008-2017.

narrative.headline: Chhatral marks the saltier western edge of the confined aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined well at Chhatral measured 1,240 mg/L dissolved solids — within the area's broadly potable range but well above fresher zones to the east. It lies in the western zone where mapping shows salinity increasing downgradient, and its Group-II confined record shows a falling trend over 2008-2017.
narrative.why_it_matters: For any use of deep groundwater here, treatment and variability are the cost drivers, not outright non-potability — and a falling confined level adds long-term yield and sustainability risk that favors monitoring, blending, or fresher eastern sources.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look east to west: lower values in the east give way to higher values around Chhatral in the west. Pair that color shift with the decade-long fall to see combined quantity and quality pressure at the western end.

insights.title: Elevated but still potable confined water
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon May 2017 sampling of the confined tube well at Chhatral recorded 1240 mg/L total dissolved solids. It was part of the GWRDC tube-well quality monitoring network used to map the User Aquifer.

insights.title: Downgradient salinity rise
insights.explanation: Regional interpretation shows confined TDS rising from about 500 mg/L in the east to more than 2700 mg/L in the west, along the east-to-west groundwater flow direction. Most of the area remains below 2000 mg/L and is described as potable, with the higher-salinity zone centered around Chhatral.

insights.title: Patchy salinity nearby
insights.explanation: Chhatral at 1240 mg/L sits between nearby Kalol stations such as Limbodara at 830 mg/L and Dingucha-I at 1590 mg/L. Co-located Dingucha wells show extreme local contrast at 1590 versus 430 mg/L, highlighting that quality can shift sharply even over short distances.

insights.title: Decade-long falling trend
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II at Chhatral, the 2008-2017 record is classified as Fall with a trend value of -0.95424, indicating a sustained declining signal over the decade alongside the quality pressure.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 confined-aquifer survey of Gandhinagar district; Chhatral station represents the western Kalol area.

narrative.headline: Dehgam-I: brackish confined water with sharp local variation after a decade of decline
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the Dehgam-I confined well recorded TDS of 810 mg/L, high compared with co-located Dehgam-III at 400 mg/L but below Dharisana at 880 mg/L. The same deep Confined Aquifer Group-II shows a 2008-2017 falling trend, while Dahegam taluka is classified as over-exploited.
narrative.why_it_matters: For a decision-maker this is a combined quantity-and-quality risk: usable deep water is present but mineralization is uneven and the aquifer has been declining under over-exploited pumping, so future supply depends more on demand control and micro-irrigation than on new recharge.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Zoom to the tight Dehgam I-II-III cluster and look for strong colour contrast between points almost on top of each other, then pull out to Dharisana to see the higher 880 mg/L shoulder.

insights.title: Premonsoon confined salinity at Dehgam-I
insights.explanation: The Dehgam-I confined well recorded 810 mg/L TDS in May 2017 pre-monsoon sampling, part of GWRDC tube-well monitoring of the user aquifer presented as a 2017 TDS map.

insights.title: Extreme local contrast in the Dehgam cluster
insights.explanation: Near-identical mapped locations diverge strongly: Dehgam-I at 810 mg/L, Dehgam-II at 750 mg/L, Dehgam-III at only 400 mg/L, while nearby Dharisana reaches 880 mg/L. This shows salinity in the confined system changes over very short distances, not as a smooth regional gradient.

insights.title: Decade-long falling signal in the deep aquifer
insights.explanation: For Confined Aquifer Group-II at Dahegam I over 2008-2017, both reported records show a Fall direction, indicating a decade-long declining signal in the same deep system that supplies this well.

insights.title: Taluka-scale over-exploitation context
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was classified as Over-Exploited (OE) in 2017 groundwater estimation, and is shown as remaining Critical even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity exceeds surplus runoff. Quality variation is therefore occurring in a quantity-stressed setting.

narrative.headline: Mid-range salinity in a stressed deep aquifer with sharp well-to-well contrasts
narrative.summary: Dehgam-II recorded 750 mg/L TDS in confined groundwater in May 2017, sitting between much fresher water at nearby Dehgam-III and saltier water at Dehgam-I and Dharisana. The same deep aquifer zone shows falling levels over 2008-2017 in a taluka assessed as over-exploited.
narrative.why_it_matters: A single moderate value is misleading here — nearby deep wells tap distinctly different water, so yield and treatment expectations cannot be transferred even over short distances. Combined with falling confined levels and an over-exploited taluka status, this favors careful, well-specific testing and demand management over assuming uniform deep supply.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the tight Dehgam I-II-III cluster: points almost on top of each other but with contrasting values, with the higher Dharisana value just to the north.

insights.title: 750 mg/L TDS in confined water at Dehgam-II
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon May 2017 sampling of the confined aquifer at Dehgam-II recorded 750 mg/L TDS. It comes from the GWRDC tube-well quality network that was mapped as the TDS of the used aquifer for pre-monsoon 2017.

insights.title: 400 to 880 mg/L variation within the Dehgam cluster
insights.explanation: Very close stations show very different results: Dehgam-I at 810 mg/L and Dharisana at 880 mg/L are higher than Dehgam-II, while Dehgam-III is much lower at 400 mg/L. The spread from 400 to 880 mg/L points to strong local heterogeneity rather than a uniform aquifer chemistry.

insights.title: Deep water levels falling over 2008-2017
insights.explanation: Two 2008-2017 records for Confined Aquifer Group-II around Dehgam are both classified as Fall, indicating declining deep water levels over the decade alongside the quality observations.

insights.title: Taluka under over-exploited groundwater status
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was categorized as OE in the 2017 groundwater assessment, projected to remain Critical even after micro-irrigation, with no artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity through structures exceeds surplus runoff. Quality therefore has to be managed under quantity stress.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of the GWRDC confined-aquifer monitoring round used to map pre-monsoon 2017 TDS of the aquifer in use.

narrative.headline: Freshest confined water in a stressed Dehgam cluster
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the confined aquifer at Dehgam-III measured 400 mg/L TDS, the lowest in its immediate group. Neighbouring Dehgam-I, Dehgam-II and Dharisana measured 750-880 mg/L. That fresher pocket sits in Dahegam taluka, classed as over-exploited in 2017.
narrative.why_it_matters: In an area with falling confined levels and over-exploitation, finding much fresher water over such a short distance points to compartmentalised quality worth protecting and tracking closely when siting or managing wells.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Dehgam-III as a low-TDS outlier amid higher-TDS points at Dehgam-I, II and Dharisana — a small fresh spot in an otherwise more saline, stressed cluster.

insights.title: Low-salinity confined measurement at Dehgam-III
insights.explanation: Pre-monsoon May 2017 sampling of the confined aquifer at Dehgam-III recorded 400 mg/L TDS. It comes from systematic tube-well quality monitoring used to map the user aquifer.

insights.title: Half the salinity of wells next door
insights.explanation: Immediate neighbours were markedly more mineralised: Dehgam-I at 810 mg/L, Dehgam-II at 750 mg/L, and Dharisana at 880 mg/L. Dehgam-III is therefore about half the salinity of wells essentially co-located with it, showing very sharp local variability.

insights.title: Nearby confined levels were falling
insights.explanation: Confined Aquifer Group-II records for nearby Dehgam-I over 2008-2017 both show a falling direction. This indicates the fresher quality at Dehgam-III coexists with declining confined pressures locally.

insights.title: Over-exploited taluka setting
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was classed as Over-Exploited for groundwater in 2017 and is shown as remaining Critical even after implementing micro-irrigation, with no artificial recharge proposed. Quality differences therefore matter in a setting with little scope to develop more water.

narrative.secondary_context: Part of GWRDC Ltd. pre-monsoon 2017 confined-aquifer TDS mapping in Gandhinagar district.

narrative.headline: Drinkable deep groundwater in an over-pumped taluka
narrative.summary: The deep tube well at Dharisana recorded 880 mg/L dissolved solids in May 2017, comfortably within the area's largely potable confined zone and on the fresher eastern side of the district. That usable quality sits inside Dahegam taluka, classified as Over-Exploited with falling levels in both shallow and deep aquifers, so the risk here is quantity rather than current salinity.
narrative.why_it_matters: The water is usable today without the high-salinity burden seen farther west, supporting domestic and irrigation use. Continued over-use and falling deep levels threaten long-term yield and could eventually pull in poorer water, so pumping control, efficiency and level monitoring matter more than immediate treatment.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map or 3D view find Dharisana in eastern Dahegam colored for moderate salinity — distinctly lighter than the high-salinity hotspot around Chhatral to the west — and note its deep 133-m confined marker versus shallower wells nearby.

insights.title: 880 mg/L in the deep aquifer before monsoon 2017
insights.explanation: GWRDC's pre-monsoon 2017 monitoring of tube wells in the used confined aquifer records 880 mg/L TDS at Dharisana. The station is described as a 133 m deep Confined-I well in the Dehgam cluster, so this is a deep-aquifer quality signal, not a shallow dug-well result.

insights.title: On the fresher side of a westward salinity gradient
insights.explanation: Across the district confined TDS ranges from about 500 mg/L to more than 2,700 mg/L, with most of the area potable at less than 2,000 mg/L. Quality is reported to deteriorate east-to-west along groundwater flow toward higher values around Chhatral in the west, placing Dharisana's 880 mg/L on the fresher, eastern side of that gradient.

insights.title: Nearby deep levels falling through 2008-2017
insights.explanation: A nearby Dahegam confined Group-II station shows a falling water-level trend over 2008-2017. That fits the broader management assessment of declining trends in both phreatic and confined aquifers in this area, meaning water-level stress even where salinity is still acceptable.

insights.title: Located in an Over-Exploited taluka
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was classified as Over-Exploited in the 2017 groundwater assessment, and remains in Critical category even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no additional artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity exceeds surplus runoff. Quantity management is therefore the dominant constraint around this well.

narrative.secondary_context: Dahegam taluka context from 2017: Over-Exploited with declining shallow and deep levels, expected to stay Critical even with micro-irrigation. The supply risk at Dharisana is sustained yield, not current salinity.

narrative.headline: Harsoli shows moderate shallow salinity in a high-stress Dehgam block
narrative.summary: The Harsoli unconfined station recorded TDS of 890 mg/L in May 2017. That is distinctly lower than nearby Dehgam highs above 1,260 mg/L, but it occurs where the shallow water table is relatively deep and the taluka is assessed as over-exploited.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning, Harsoli signals usable-but-not-fresh shallow water in an area where groundwater demand already exceeds sustainable limits, making both salinity variation and long-term level reliability important to watch.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map view, look for Harsoli in Dehgam taluka as a mid-range point — less intense than the higher-salinity points to the south and northeast — sitting within the 10-50 m shallow-level zone.

insights.title: May-2017 shallow TDS of 890 mg/L
insights.explanation: A May-2017 sample from the unconfined aquifer at Harsoli, Dehgam taluka, reported TDS of 890 mg/L. It comes from the district's groundwater monitoring network analysis for the unconfined aquifer in May 2017.

insights.title: Lower than nearby Dehgam highs
insights.explanation: Harsoli is fresher than two nearby Dehgam unconfined stations sampled in the same period: Hilol at 1,260 mg/L and Kadjodra at 1,320 mg/L. That places Harsoli in the middle of the local range rather than at the high-salinity hotspot.

insights.title: Deep shallow water table setting
insights.explanation: The source map places eastern and western areas including Dahegam in a 10-50 metres below ground level phreatic zone for pre-monsoon May-2017. A separate monitoring piezometer at Harsoli recorded a static water level of 46.85 m in July 2014, consistent with a relatively deep shallow water table here.

insights.title: Quantity stress in the same block
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was categorized as Over-Exploited in the 2017 groundwater estimation and as Critical even after accounting for micro-irrigation, with no artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity exceeded surplus runoff. Quality at Harsoli therefore needs to be read alongside quantity stress, not in isolation.

narrative.secondary_context: Shallow groundwater quality and levels in this district are tracked through a dedicated monitoring network, including confined-aquifer TDS mapping by GWRDC Ltd.

narrative.headline: Hilol records near-maximum salinity in Dehgam's stressed shallow aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the shallow well at Hilol recorded 1,260 mg/L dissolved solids, among the highest values in Gandhinagar district that season. It sits in Dehgam, where shallow groundwater is relatively accessible at 10-50 metres depth but the block is already over-exploited.
narrative.why_it_matters: Saltier water in an already over-used block means less usable supply without treatment or demand management, raising operating risk for any water-dependent use. This is a location to plan for quality constraints and close monitoring rather than expanded shallow extraction.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Hilol in eastern Dehgam as a high-value spot rising from lower values to the west; overlay water levels and block status to see shallow depth coinciding with high salinity and extraction stress.

insights.title: High dissolved solids at Hilol
insights.explanation: The Hilol monitoring station in Dehgam taluka recorded 1,260 mg/L total dissolved solids in the unconfined aquifer in May 2017, a pre-monsoon snapshot from the district groundwater quality network.

insights.title: Near the top of the district range
insights.explanation: Hilol is just below the highest May-2017 value at nearby Kadjodra at 1,320 mg/L, and well above nearby Harsoli at 890 mg/L and Karai at 580 mg/L, placing it at the salty end of the district's 350 to 1,320 mg/L range.

insights.title: Shallow but salty
insights.explanation: Hilol lies in the eastern zone where the May-2017 phreatic water level was 10-50 metres below ground, shallower than the 50-70 metre zone in central Gandhinagar and northern Mansa — so water is relatively accessible but quality is already mineralized.

insights.title: Over-stressed groundwater block
insights.explanation: Dehgam taluka was classed as over-exploited in 2017 and remains in the critical category even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no additional artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity already exceeds surplus runoff.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 snapshot of the unconfined aquifer; part of district-wide monitoring of shallow wells and deeper tube wells.

narrative.headline: Karai records fresher shallow groundwater amid saltier neighbours
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the unconfined aquifer at Karai measured 580 mg/L TDS. That is among the lowest values in the surrounding set, well below eastern stations that exceed 1,000 mg/L, and close to neighboring Koteshwar at 490 mg/L.
narrative.why_it_matters: For siting and risk screening, Karai indicates a relatively better-quality shallow zone at that time, while the sharp rise nearby shows quality can change over short distances and warrants localized checking.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Karai as a lower-value point in the west-central area, contrasting with larger, saltier signals to the east around Hilol, Kadjodra and Antroli.

insights.title: 580 mg/L TDS at Karai in May 2017
insights.explanation: The May-2017 unconfined observation at Karai in Gandhinagar taluka is 580 mg/L TDS, a pre-monsoon snapshot of the shallow aquifer at this point.

insights.title: Much lower than the eastern Dehgam cluster
insights.explanation: Nearby stations to the east and southeast are markedly saltier: Harsoli at 890 mg/L, Magodi at 1060 mg/L, Antroli at 1130 mg/L, Hilol at 1260 mg/L, and Kadjodra at 1320 mg/L — roughly 1.5 to more than 2 times the Karai value.

insights.title: Part of a fresher western pocket
insights.explanation: Karai groups with a fresher western side that includes Koteshwar at 490 mg/L and Patnakuva at 700 mg/L, suggesting a west-to-east increase in mineralization across this part of Gandhinagar district in May 2017.

narrative.headline: Koteshwar was the freshest shallow well in the May 2017 round
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the unconfined aquifer at Koteshwar measured 490 mg/L dissolved solids, the lowest value in this Gandhinagar-area group. Nearby shallow wells ranged from 580 mg/L at Karai to over 1,300 mg/L in eastern Dehgam, marking Koteshwar as a distinct low-salinity pocket.
narrative.why_it_matters: Shallow salinity changes sharply over short distances here, so this fresher pocket stands out for future supply and monitoring choices — conditions near Koteshwar are much less mineralized than the ground to the east.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Koteshwar as the low-value point in the west, contrasting with progressively higher values stretching east toward Dehgam.

insights.title: Pre-monsoon shallow TDS of 490 mg/L
insights.explanation: Direct May-2017 observation from the unconfined aquifer at Koteshwar reported 490 mg/L dissolved solids, establishing the baseline for this station.

insights.title: Freshest in its survey neighbourhood
insights.explanation: Nearby Karai measured 580 mg/L and Patnakuva 700 mg/L, while Harsoli reached 890 mg/L and Magodi 1,060 mg/L. Farther east, Antroli at 1,130 mg/L, Hilol at 1,260 mg/L and Kadjodra at 1,320 mg/L were more than twice as mineralized as Koteshwar.

insights.title: Western low-salinity edge
insights.explanation: Koteshwar lies in Gandhinagar taluka in the west of this group, while the highest-salinity readings cluster to the east in Dehgam taluka, creating a clear west-to-east increase in shallow groundwater mineralization.

narrative.secondary_context: Single-season May 2017 snapshot of the unconfined aquifer in Gandhinagar district.

narrative.headline: A relatively fresher shallow well in Dehgam's over-used aquifer
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the Patnakuva unconfined station recorded TDS of 700 mg/L, distinctly lower than nearby Dehgam stations ranging up to 1320 mg/L. It sits in a 10-50 metre pre-monsoon water-level zone, but in a taluka classified as over-exploited, so relative quality strength coexists with quantity pressure.
narrative.why_it_matters: For an investor, lower dissolved solids suggest lower treatment and usability friction at this spot, but the taluka-level over-exploitation status means future availability depends more on pumping and recharge management than on this single quality reading.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Patnakuva as a lower-TDS point in northern Dehgam amid higher values to the south, within the broader shallow 10-50 metre water-level belt.

insights.title: May 2017 shallow TDS at Patnakuva
insights.explanation: The Patnakuva station in Dehgam taluka recorded 700 in the unconfined aquifer in May-2017, conventionally reported as mg/L. It comes from the district's May 2017 unconfined-aquifer monitoring round presented as Table 13.

insights.title: Fresher than nearby Dehgam stations
insights.explanation: Patnakuva at 700 sits well below other May-2017 Dehgam unconfined records in the same table: Harsoli at 890, Hilol at 1260, and Kadjodra at 1320. In the map view this makes Patnakuva in the north look like a fresher pocket compared with saltier points to the south.

insights.title: Shallower water table, but stressed balance
insights.explanation: In May-2017 the phreatic surface in Dahegam and Kalol was interpreted at 10-50 metres below ground level, shallower than the 50-70 metre zone in central Gandhinagar. At the same time Dahegam was classed as OE for 2017 groundwater extraction, remaining Critical even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, so quantity stress frames any quality advantage.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May-2017 snapshot of the unconfined aquifer only; not a trend or confined-aquifer signal.

narrative.headline: High-salinity shallow groundwater at Antroli in an over-extracted Dehgam pocket
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the Antroli unconfined station in Dehgam recorded TDS of 1,130 mg/L. It sits within a cluster of high-TDS shallow results in Dehgam ranging from 890 to 1,320 mg/L, in an area of relatively shallower pre-monsoon levels but over-exploited extraction status.
narrative.why_it_matters: Shallow water here is more mineralized, which narrows direct-use options without treatment and adds cost and risk for any operation relying on shallow supply. Combined with over-exploited status, it signals that future reliability will depend less on the shallow zone and more on deeper sources, treatment, or managed demand.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Antroli in eastern Dehgam and look for its high-value marker clustering with Hilol and Kadjodra to the south and east; compare with lower markers like Harsoli to see the local salinity hotspot.

insights.title: Pre-monsoon shallow TDS of 1,130 mg/L at Antroli
insights.explanation: The Antroli station in Dehgam taluka recorded 1,130 mg/L TDS in the unconfined aquifer in May 2017. It comes from the district's pre-monsoon unconfined-aquifer monitoring round, so it represents dry-season shallow quality before recharge.

insights.title: Part of a high-TDS cluster in Dehgam
insights.explanation: Antroli is not an outlier: nearby Dehgam villages in the same May-2017 round show 890 mg/L at Harsoli, 1,260 mg/L at Hilol, and 1,320 mg/L at Kadjodra. Together they define a locally saline shallow zone where Antroli sits in the middle-high range.

insights.title: Shallower water levels but poor quality
insights.explanation: Dehgam falls in the eastern district zone where pre-monsoon phreatic levels in May 2017 were mapped at 10-50 metres below ground level, shallower than the 50-70 metre zone in central Gandhinagar. At Antroli, water is relatively accessible in depth but carries high dissolved load.

insights.title: Over-extracted taluka setting
insights.explanation: Dehgam (Dahegam) was classed as OE - over-exploited - in the 2017 groundwater estimation, and remains in Critical category even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity exceeds surplus runoff. Quality stress at Antroli therefore coincides with quantitative stress.

narrative.secondary_context: May 2017 is a pre-monsoon snapshot of the phreatic/unconfined system; confined/user-aquifer quality in the district is monitored separately.

narrative.headline: Magodi shallow water is moderately saline, sitting between fresher west and saltier east
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the unconfined aquifer at Magodi recorded 1060 mg/L dissolved solids. That places it above fresher shallow wells to the west but below the most mineralized wells to the east, highlighting sharp local variation in shallow groundwater quality.
narrative.why_it_matters: Shallow groundwater near Magodi is significantly more mineralized than water a short distance west, so any shallow-well use here should allow for testing and treatment or blending for saltiness rather than assuming fresher conditions. The tight geographic contrast also means exact well location matters for future water planning.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Magodi in the middle of the Gandhinagar cluster — higher than the pale western points at Karai and Koteshwar, but lower than the darkest eastern points — illustrating the west-to-east salinity rise.

insights.title: May 2017 unconfined TDS at Magodi: 1060 mg/L
insights.explanation: A direct May-17 observation in the unconfined aquifer at Magodi, Gandhinagar taluka, reported 1060 mg/L total dissolved solids. This is the anchor value for this station and indicates distinctly mineralized, salty-tasting shallow groundwater at that time.

insights.title: Higher than the west, lower than the eastern highs
insights.explanation: Magodi is about double the fresher wells to the west — Karai at 580 mg/L and Koteshwar at 490 mg/L — and well above Patnakuva to the north at 700 mg/L and Harsoli at 890 mg/L. It is close to Antroli at 1130 mg/L, but below the highest nearby values at Hilol at 1260 mg/L and Kadjodra at 1320 mg/L to the east and southeast.

insights.title: Part of a patchy district-scale salinity pattern
insights.explanation: All wells are unconfined May-17 records in Gandhinagar district across Gandhinagar and Dehgam talukas. Magodi at 23.2N, 72.77E sits in the middle of a west-to-east rise, from under 600 mg/L in the west to over 1100-1300 mg/L in the east, showing that shallow quality changes sharply over short distances.

narrative.headline: Valad shallow water is saltier than its western neighbours yet holding steady
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the unconfined aquifer at Valad measured 970 mg/L dissolved solids. That puts it above nearby Karai and Koteshwar to the west but below the highest May-2017 values east in Dehgam. Over 2008-2017 its shallow level shows a slight rising tendency, unlike about half the district's wells that were declining.
narrative.why_it_matters: For any shallow-well use here, mineral load is the main variable to plan around for treatment or choice of use, while the flat-to-slightly-rising level history suggests quantity has not been deteriorating like in declining pockets nearby.
narrative.visual_takeaway: In the map view find Valad between the lower-TDS points to the west and the higher-TDS points to the east; it marks the transition where quality worsens eastward even as levels remain stable.

insights.title: May 2017 shallow TDS at Valad
insights.explanation: The May 2017 direct record for the unconfined aquifer at Valad is 970 mg/L total dissolved solids, defining it as moderately mineralized shallow groundwater at this location.

insights.title: Mid-range in a west-to-east salinity pattern
insights.explanation: Valad sits in the middle of a west-to-east gradient: lower than Hilol at 1260 mg/L and Kadjodra at 1320 mg/L to the east in Dehgam, but higher than Karai at 580 mg/L and Koteshwar at 490 mg/L to the west in Gandhinagar, and also above Harsoli at 890 mg/L and Patnakuva at 700 mg/L.

insights.title: Slight long-term rise amid a mixed district trend
insights.explanation: Taluka-wise analysis of unconfined wells for 2008-2017 found 50% declining and 50% rising. Valad is at the low end of the rising group at +0.0229 m/year, indicating essentially stable to slightly recovering levels rather than the declines seen down to -0.9286 m/year elsewhere.

narrative.headline: Mubarakpura shows mineralized shallow groundwater in Kalol's over-exploited, regulated zone
narrative.summary: At Mubarakpura in Kalol taluka, the May 2017 unconfined sample recorded TDS of 1,130 mg/L. The station lies in the eastern 10-50 metre pre-monsoon water-level belt, within a taluka assessed as Over-Exploited and regulated for groundwater abstraction since 2012.
narrative.why_it_matters: Shallow water here carries both quality and quantity risk: mineralization shapes treatment and use options, while Notified-Area controls and over-exploited status mean new abstraction needs approval and long-term supply depends on recharge and demand management.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find the shallow unconfined point at Mubarakpura in eastern Kalol — a 10-50 m water-level zone — marked by its 1,130 mg/L May-2017 TDS signal inside a taluka-wide over-development and notified-area backdrop.

insights.title: May 2017 unconfined TDS: 1,130 mg/L
insights.explanation: The station at Mubarakpura, Kalol taluka (23.35N, 72.68E) is listed as an Unconfined monitoring station with TDS reported as 1130.0 for MAY-17. It comes from the May 2017 Table 13 analysis for the Unconfined Aquifer.

insights.title: Shallow pre-monsoon water-level belt
insights.explanation: The source map interpretation places eastern and western district including Kalol in 10-50 metres below ground level in pre-monsoon May-2017, versus 50-70 m in central Gandhinagar, NW Kalol and northern Mansa. Mubarakpura therefore sits in the shallower phreatic belt, not the deep central trough.

insights.title: 2008-2017 record preserved as rise
insights.explanation: The 2008-2017 source table row for Kalol-Mubarakpura-Unconfined preserves a rise flag for the period, in contrast to fall flags recorded elsewhere. The printed magnitude is poorly formatted, so only the direction is interpreted, not a precise rate.

insights.title: Regulated and over-exploited taluka setting
insights.explanation: Kalol Taluka was declared a Notified Area for regulation of groundwater abstraction in 2012, requiring prior approval of the Authorized Officer with safeguards and rainwater harvesting. It was assessed as OE with extraction stage listed as 114.08 in 2017, improving only to Critical after assumed micro-irrigation, within a district assessed at 113.55% and classed Over Exploited.

narrative.secondary_context: Kalol: Notified Area since 27-11-2012; 2017 extraction stage 114.08 (OE), 99.63 (Critical) after micro-irrigation intervention; Gandhinagar district 113.55% Over Exploited with taluka range 104.02-139.35%.

narrative.headline: Fresher water at Bilodra, but sitting in a falling, heavily used water table
narrative.summary: Bilodra's shallow groundwater measured 410 mg/L TDS in May 2017, fresher than Delvad's 500 mg/L nearby. That quality signal sits alongside a persistent quantity stress: about 0.79 m per year of fall from 2008-2017 in an area of deep 50-70 m pre-monsoon levels and taluka-wide over-extraction.
narrative.why_it_matters: For planning, the site offers no current salinity hotspot, but the falling trend and over-extracted taluka status mean future availability and pumping depth, not quality alone, are the main risk to watch.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Bilodra in northern Mansa as a lower-TDS point inside the deeper water-level zone — quality looks better locally while the long-term level arrow points down.

insights.title: May 2017 unconfined quality measurement
insights.explanation: The station recorded 410 mg/L TDS in the unconfined aquifer in the May 2017 pre-monsoon round, part of the district Table 13 groundwater-quality monitoring for the unconfined aquifer.

insights.title: Relatively fresher than nearby Delvad
insights.explanation: Nearby Delvad in the same Mansa taluka recorded 500 mg/L in the same round, making Bilodra about 90 mg/L lower and the fresher of this local pair.

insights.title: Steady decade-long water-level fall
insights.explanation: The source table lists Bilodra unconfined as -0.7886 (Fall) for 2008-2017. That is near the steep end of the district's declining group, which ranged to -0.9286, while the other half of wells were rising.

insights.title: Deep levels in an over-extracted taluka
insights.explanation: In May 2017, northern Mansa was mapped in the deeper 50-70 mbgl phreatic zone, versus 10-50 mbgl in the east and west. Mansa taluka as a whole is classed OE in the 2017 assessment and remains OE even under the micro-irrigation intervention scenario.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 CGWB and GWRDC monitoring for Gandhinagar district; Mansa shows mixed signals with rising levels elsewhere such as Amrapur alongside Bilodra's decline.

narrative.headline: A relatively fresh pocket persisting in Mansa's deep, over-used water table
narrative.summary: In May 2017 the Delvad unconfined well recorded TDS of 500 mg/L, slightly above Bilodra at 410 mg/L in the same taluka. It sits in northern Mansa where pre-monsoon levels were 50-70 m deep and extraction is classified as over-exploited, yet its 2008-2017 record is listed as rising.
narrative.why_it_matters: Delvad shows quality and quantity decoupling here: water stays on the fresher side even where the water table is deep and use exceeds recharge. Sustaining that pocket depends more on managing levels and pumping than on addressing salinity.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Find Delvad in northern Mansa and compare it with Bilodra nearby, then overlay depth-to-water and trend: fresher quality overlapping deep levels but with a rising signal.

insights.title: Pre-monsoon fresher-water reading at Delvad
insights.explanation: The Delvad station in Mansa taluka recorded TDS of 500 mg/L in the May 2017 pre-monsoon round for the unconfined aquifer, part of the district-wide groundwater monitoring programme for that season.

insights.title: Close to Bilodra, slightly higher
insights.explanation: Nearby Bilodra in the same taluka recorded 410 mg/L in the same round, so Delvad is slightly more mineralised but still in the same lower-TDS band, showing short-distance variability rather than a sharp saline front.

insights.title: Long-term level signal is rising, not falling
insights.explanation: The source table lists Delvad unconfined for 2008-2017 as a rise, against a district pattern where half the unconfined wells fell and half rose. This sets Delvad apart from declining wells elsewhere in the same period.

insights.title: Rise inside a deep, stressed zone
insights.explanation: That rise occurs where pre-monsoon unconfined levels in northern Mansa were interpreted as 50-70 metres below ground, and where Mansa taluka is categorised as over-exploited both in 2017 and after a modelled micro-irrigation intervention, with extraction still exceeding recharge.

narrative.secondary_context: May 2017 pre-monsoon sampling covered the unconfined aquifer; deeper user-aquifer quality from tube wells was mapped separately.

narrative.headline: District's freshest shallow groundwater in a heavily pumped alluvial pocket
narrative.summary: This station recorded 350 mg/L TDS in May 2017, the lowest unconfined value district-wide, indicating relatively fresh groundwater. The same village shows deepening October levels and negative 2008-2017 trends in alluvium within a taluka assessed as over-exploited to critical.
narrative.why_it_matters: Fresh water lowers treatment and usability constraints, but falling levels and taluka-scale over-exploitation create reliability and cost risk for any supply-dependent plan.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for the low-salinity spot near 23.13N, 72.96E in Dehgam — then toggle to water levels to see deep, downward-trending blues beneath that fresh signal.

insights.title: Freshest May-2017 unconfined reading
insights.explanation: May-2017 sampling of the unconfined aquifer at Devkaran-na-muvada recorded 350 mg/L TDS as part of the district groundwater monitoring network for the unconfined aquifer.

insights.title: How it compares across the district
insights.explanation: That 350 mg/L value is the minimum for the May-2017 unconfined set, standing well below peers that reach 1,320 mg/L and include values of 1,260, 1,130, 890 and 700 mg/L. For a non-technical viewer, this is the low-salinity outlier on the quality map.

insights.title: Levels falling while quality stays fresh
insights.explanation: Two nearby unconfined records for the same village carry negative 2008-2017 trends of -0.6023 and -0.2850. October post-monsoon levels deepened from about 10.1 m in 2007 to 15.2 m in 2017 in the shallow record and from 17.8 m to 23.2 m in the deeper record, against decadal averages of 12.96 m and 21.66 m, with negative reported fluctuations.

insights.title: Alluvial setting with paired depths
insights.explanation: Both village records are in alluvium at about 82 m ground elevation, but tap different depths: one drilled to 19.5 m and one to 55 m. In 3D, expect a shallow and a deeper completion stacked at almost the same location, helping explain why water-table depths differ.

insights.title: Over-used regional context
insights.explanation: The station sits in Dehgam/Dahegam taluka, where pre-monsoon May-2017 phreatic depths are typically 10-50 m below ground. The taluka was assessed as over-exploited in 2017 and remains in critical category even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no additional artificial recharge proposed because recharge capacity exceeds surplus runoff. A July-2014 monitoring piezometer in the village stood at 28.97 m, consistent with a deep water-table area.

narrative.secondary_context: Dahegam taluka's over-exploited to critical assessment means fresh quality here does not imply spare quantity.

narrative.headline: A fresher shallow well in Dehgam's heavily used aquifer
narrative.summary: The Jindva unconfined station recorded 660 mg/L TDS in May 2017, distinctly fresher than nearby Dehgam wells that reached 890-1,320 mg/L. It lies in the 10-50 m pre-monsoon water-level belt, but Dahegam taluka as a whole was over-exploited in 2017.
narrative.why_it_matters: For siting or diligence, Jindva points to a locally fresher shallow pocket, yet any use depends on managing quantity in an over-exploited taluka where neighbouring quality varies sharply over short distances.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for Jindva as a lower-TDS point among higher values clustered to its south in Dehgam, within the shallower eastern water-level zone.

insights.title: May-2017 shallow TDS at Jindva
insights.explanation: This station recorded 660 mg/L TDS in the unconfined aquifer in May 2017, part of the district-wide groundwater monitoring round for unconfined aquifers presented for that month.

insights.title: Fresher than nearby Dehgam wells
insights.explanation: Nearby Dehgam stations in the same May-2017 round were saltier: Harsoli at 890 mg/L, Hilol at 1,260 mg/L, and Kadjodra at 1,320 mg/L, making Jindva about half the mineral load of its closest high-TDS neighbours.

insights.title: Shallower water, but stressed taluka
insights.explanation: Jindva sits in the eastern/western pre-monsoon zone where phreatic levels were 10-50 metres below ground in May 2017, shallower than central areas at 50-70 m. At the taluka scale, Dahegam was classed as over-exploited in 2017, improving only to Critical even with micro-irrigation, so quantity stress remains the broader constraint.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 snapshot of the unconfined aquifer; quality is one signal alongside water-level and extraction pressure.

narrative.headline: Sanoda is a freshwater pocket in over-used Dehgam
narrative.summary: Sanoda's unconfined well showed 410 mg/L TDS in May 2017, among the freshest results in Dehgam versus 890-1,260 mg/L nearby. That relatively good quality occurs in shallow alluvium in a taluka assessed as over-exploited and still critical after efficiency gains.
narrative.why_it_matters: A fresh, shallow resource in an over-pumped block is both an opportunity and a risk — valuable for local supply but vulnerable to decline or salinity ingress if extraction continues without management.
narrative.visual_takeaway: Look for a low-salinity point at northern Dehgam around Sanoda contrasting with warmer, higher-TDS points to the south around Harsoli and Hilol.

insights.title: Fresh May-2017 result at Sanoda
insights.explanation: The station recorded 410 mg/L TDS in the unconfined aquifer in May 2017, part of the district-wide pre-monsoon groundwater quality survey of the unconfined aquifer.

insights.title: Sharply fresher than neighbours
insights.explanation: Nearby Dehgam villages in the same May-2017 round were much saltier: Harsoli at 890 mg/L and Hilol at 1,260 mg/L, making Sanoda about one-half to one-third their salinity and near the fresh end of the district.

insights.title: Typical shallow alluvial water levels
insights.explanation: Sanoda sits in alluvium with ground elevation around 82 m and 88 m drilled depth. Its decadal-average level around 38.5 m and October 2017 level of 33.3 m fit the mapped pre-monsoon phreatic pattern for Dahegam and Kalol of 10-50 metres below ground level.

insights.title: Good quality in a stressed block
insights.explanation: Dahegam taluka was classed as Over-Exploited in the 2017 groundwater assessment and remains Critical even after assumed micro-irrigation savings, with no new artificial-recharge capacity proposed from surplus runoff.

narrative.secondary_context: Pre-monsoon May 2017 survey; deeper tube-wells were monitored separately for the confined user aquifer.
